questions.knowledge_point: Differentiating a Quotient of Two Polynomials
questions.worked_solution:
The numerator and denominator are $u(x)=1$ and $v(x)=x+1,$ respectively. Their derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′}(x) & =0, \\ {v}^{′}(x) & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the quotient rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{0\cdot (x+1)-1\cdot 1}{{(x+1)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-1}{{(x+1)}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{{(x+1)}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The numerator and denominator are $u(x)={x}^{2}$ and $v(x)=x+1,$ respectively. Their derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′}(x) & =2x, \\ {v}^{′}(x) & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the quotient rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2x\cdot (x+1)-{x}^{2}\cdot 1}{{(x+1)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2{x}^{2}+2x-{x}^{2}}{{(x+1)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}+2x}{(x+1)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
The numerator and denominator are $u(x)=x$ and $v(x)={x}^{2}+1,$ respectively. Their derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′}(x) & =1, \\ {v}^{′}(x) & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the quotient rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1\cdot ({x}^{2}+1)-x\cdot (2x)}{{({x}^{2}+1)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}+1-2{x}^{2}}{({x}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1-{x}^{2}}{({x}^{2}+1)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{6\cdot (1-3x)-6x\cdot (-3)}{{(1-3x)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{6-18x+18x}{{(1-3x)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{6}{{(1-3x)}^{2}}.\end{aligned}

$$

questions.knowledge_point: Differentiating a Quotient Containing Other Functions
questions.problem:
If a curve $C$ is given by $y=\frac{{2}^{x}}{{x}^{2}-1},$ calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $x=0.$

The slope at $x=0$ is
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
In this case, the expression for $y$ is a quotient $\frac{u(x)}{v(x)}$ with $u(x)={2}^{x}$ and $v(x)={x}^{2}-1.$ 

Therefore, we apply the quotient rule as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{({2}^{x})}^{′}\cdot ({x}^{2}-1)-{2}^{x}\cdot {({x}^{2}-1)}^{′}}{{({x}^{2}-1)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{2}^{x}ln⁡2\cdot ({x}^{2}-1)-{2}^{x}\cdot 2x}{{({x}^{2}-1)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{{2}^{x}[({x}^{2}-1)ln⁡2-2x]}{{({x}^{2}-1)}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=0$ into the formula and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\,(0) & =\frac{{2}^{0}[({0}^{2}-1)ln⁡2-2(0)]}{{({0}^{2}-1)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-ln⁡2}{1} \\  & =-ln⁡2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line at $x=0$ is $-ln⁡2.$

questions.problem: If a curve $C$ is given by $y=\frac{{x}^{2}}{ln⁡(x)},$ calculate the slope of the tangent line to the curve at the point where $x=e.$
questions.worked_solution:
In this case, the expression for $y$ is a quotient $\frac{u(x)}{v(x)}$ with $u(x)={x}^{2}$ and $v(x)=ln⁡x.$ 

Therefore, we apply the quotient rule as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2})^{′}\cdot ln⁡x-{x}^{2}\cdot (ln⁡x)^{′}}{(ln⁡x)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2x\cdot ln⁡(x)-{x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1}{x})}{{(ln⁡(x))}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2x\cdot ln⁡(x)-x}{{ln}^{2}⁡(x)} \\  & =\frac{x(2ln⁡(x)-1)}{{ln}^{2}⁡(x)}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the slope of the tangent line, we now substitute $x=e$ into the formula and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(e) & =\frac{e(2ln⁡(e)-1)}{{ln}^{2}⁡(e)} \\  & =\frac{e(2-1)}{{1}^{2}} \\  & =e.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent line is $e.$

questions.knowledge_point: Differentiating a Quotient Using Leibniz Notation
questions.worked_solution:
Let $u=x$ and $v=cos⁡x.$ Then

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =1\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=-sin⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quotient rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}-u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}}{{v}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{cos⁡x\cdot 1-x\cdot (-sin⁡x)}{{cos}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{1}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}\cdot (cos⁡x+xsin⁡x\,).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Differentiating a Quotient Using Leibniz Notation
questions.worked_solution:
Let $u=-x$ and $v=9-2x.$ Then

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =-1\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quotient rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}-u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}}{{v}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(9-2x)\cdot (-1)-(-x)\cdot (-2)}{{(9-2x)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{-9+2x-2x}{{(9-2x)}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{9}{{(9-2x)}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Differentiating a Quotient Using Leibniz Notation
questions.worked_solution:
Let $u={log}_{3}⁡x=\frac{ln⁡x}{ln⁡3}$ and $v={x}^{2}.$ Then

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{xln⁡3}\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quotient rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}-u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}}{{v}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{({x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{xln⁡3}-\frac{ln⁡x}{ln⁡3}\cdot 2x)}{({x}^{2})^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{x}{ln⁡3}-\frac{2xln⁡x}{ln⁡3})}{{x}^{4}} \\  & =\frac{x-2xln⁡x}{{x}^{4}ln⁡3} \\  & =\frac{x(1-2ln⁡x)}{{x}^{4}ln⁡3} \\  & =\frac{1-2ln⁡x}{{x}^{3}ln⁡3} \\  & =(\,1-2ln⁡x\,)\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{3}ln⁡3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Differentiating a Quotient Using Leibniz Notation
questions.worked_solution:
Let $u=1-sin⁡x$ and $v=sin⁡x.$ Then

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-cos⁡x\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=cos⁡x.
$$

Using the quotient rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}-u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}}{{v}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{sin⁡x\cdot (-cos⁡x)-(1-sin⁡x)\cdot cos⁡x}{{sin}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{cos⁡x(-sin⁡x-1+sin⁡x)}{{sin}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =\frac{cos⁡x\cdot (-1)}{{sin}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =-\frac{1}{sin⁡x}\cdot \frac{cos⁡x}{sin⁡x} \\  & =-csc⁡xcot⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Differentiating a Quotient Using Leibniz Notation
questions.worked_solution:
Let $u=x$ and $v=ln⁡x.$ Then

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =1\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quotient rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}-u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}}{{v}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(ln⁡x\cdot 1-x\cdot \frac{1}{x})}{{(ln⁡x)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{ln⁡x-1}{{(ln⁡x)}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Differentiating a Quotient of Two Polynomials
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The numerator and denominator are $u(x) = x$ and $v(x) = 9x^2 + 5x,$ respectively. Their derivatives are given by

 

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}^{′}(x) & =1, \\ {v}^{′}(x) & =18x+5.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the quotient rule, we have

$$
\eqalign{
			f'(x) 	& = \dfrac {u'(x)\cdot v(x) - u(x) v'(x)} {[v(x)]^2}\
				& = \dfrac{\left( 9x^2+5x \right )\cdot 1 -x\cdot \left( 18x+5 \right)}{\left( 9x^2+5x\right)^2}\
				& = \dfrac{\left( 9x^2+5x-18x^2-5x \right)}{\left( 9x^2+5x\right)^2}\
				& = -\dfrac{9x^2}{\left( 9x^2+5x\right)^2}.
		}
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $u=1$ and $v=3x+7.$ Then

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} & =0\,\text{and}\,\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=3.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quotient rule, we get

$$
\eqalign{
			\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}	& = \dfrac{ v\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}-u\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x}}{v^2}\
										& = \dfrac{ \left( 3x+7 \right ) \cdot 0 -1\cdot 3}{\left( 3x+7\right)^2}\
										& = -\dfrac{3}{\left( 3x+7\right)^2}.
		}
$$
